pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Top Blocks: Change on Church and Cherry, by Alexander Tolstoi, 2017

timeline.detail: W.S. Rann's 1886 county history notes an inn on the corner before the 1800s, which Rann believed Harvey Durkee owned. His widow Dolly later ran it and sold it to Henry Stanton.
timeline.quote: an inn had been on the corner before the 1800’s which Rann believed was owned by Harvey Durkee

timeline.what: Ell-shaped building on Ammi Young map
timeline.detail: The earliest depiction of the corner building is Ammi Young's 1830 map, which shows an ell-shaped building.
timeline.quote: the earliest depiction is Ammi Young’s hand drawn map from 1830 which does depict an ell-shaped building on the corner of Church and Cherry Streets

timeline.detail: Henry Stanton opened a hotel on the corner in 1859. The page says he would build it, and also that he bought the property from Dolly Durkee.
timeline.quote: In 1859, Henry Stanton would build a hotel on the corner of Church and Cherry Streets

timeline.detail: R.C. Rowe took over in 1874, renamed it Rowe's Hotel and closed it for three weeks of repairs. He sold in 1889.
timeline.quote: Changing hands again in 1874, the new proprietor of the hotel, R.C. Rowe, would change the name to Rowe’s Hotel and shut down the business for three weeks for extensive repairs.

timeline.detail: G.M. Hopkins bought the property in 1889 and briefly ran it as Hotel Chittenden, a boarding hotel often in police reports.
timeline.quote: selling the property in 1889 to G.M. Hopkins who briefly ran the business under the name Hotel Chittenden

timeline.detail: The Hotel Chittenden became the Sherwood Hotel in the 1890s.
timeline.quote: The switch from Hotel Chittenden to the Sherwood Hotel in the 1890’s happened as Burlington was at its economic peak.

timeline.detail: After an 1895 fire the Sherwood was rebuilt as a four-story brick building.
timeline.quote: Following a fire in 1895 the Sherwood was completely rebuilt as a four-story brick building, anchoring the corner of Church and Cherry Streets.

timeline.detail: Around the turn of the century E.H. Vancor sold electrical equipment on the hotel's ground floor.
timeline.quote: On the ground floor of the hotel, E.H. Vancor sold electrical equipment; wires, call bells and other “electrics”.

timeline.detail: The seven-story New Sherwood, designed by Frank Lyman Austin, was completed in summer 1912 with shops, a restaurant and a moving-picture hall.
timeline.quote: Completed in the summer of 1912, the seven-story hotel designed by Vermont architect Frank Lyman Austin featured various shops, a restaurant and even a “moving-picture hall” on the second floor.

timeline.detail: By April 1914 P.T. Donovan sold Oakland and Oldsmobile cars from the New Sherwood's Cherry Street side.
timeline.quote: As early as April of 1914, Donovan was selling Oakland’s “the car with a conscience” and the 1915 Oldsmobile for only $1,285.

timeline.detail: The Milner Hotel company leased the New Sherwood in 1938.
timeline.quote: The Milner Hotel company would lease the New Sherwood Hotel in 1938 but their ownership would prove short lived.

timeline.detail: A fire on February 14, 1940 leveled the seven-story hotel. All 160 patrons were saved.
timeline.quote: On Valentine’s Day 1940 a devastating fire ripped through the 29-35 Church Street leveling the seven-story building.

timeline.detail: Sears and Roebuck built a two-story, 16,000 square foot brick building in 1941, occupied by J.C. Penney until it left in the 1980s.
timeline.quote: Sears and Roebuck would move to Shelburne, but would rebuild on their Church Street property in 1941. The new two-story, 16,000 square foot brick building would be occupied by J.C. Penny’s Department Store.

timeline.detail: Borders completely renovated the building in 1993, adding an open staircase that a later tenant removed.
timeline.quote: The national bookstore chain Borders would completely renovate 29-35 Church Street in 1993, adding a large open staircase in the middle of the store

timeline.detail: A house stood here, home first to Mrs. Grant and then Mrs. Ann Williams, between Stanton's House and a grocery.
timeline.quote: there was still evidence of a Mrs. Grant and subsequently a Mrs. Ann Williams living at 25 Church, between Stanton’s House and a grocery.

timeline.detail: Mrs. Williams sold to P.H. Corley in 1885, who built the three-story brick building that still stands. Corley sold groceries, Catholic books and stationery.
timeline.quote: Land records show that it was Mrs. Williams who sold the property to P.H Corley in 1885 who would build the three-story brick building that stands today.

timeline.detail: Corley's store became People's Department Store, which the page calls the start of chain stores on the block in 1895.
timeline.quote: in reality it started back in 1895 with People’s Department Store.

timeline.detail: Architect Benjamin Stein designed the large glass wall for Mayfair Department Store in 1972.
timeline.quote: in 1972 with architect Benjamin Stein’s large glass wall design for Mayfair Department store at 25-27 Church Street that we see today.

timeline.detail: After so many renovations the building was deemed noncontributing in the 2010 historic district nomination.
timeline.quote: the building was deemed noncontributing to the National Historic District Nomination in 2010.

photos.caption: Then and now; the top photo is from the 1950s

timeline.detail: Hiram Blood bought the dwelling north of Stanton's house in 1861 and rebuilt it as a grocery. Parts of that store may survive, making it possibly the oldest building on the block.
timeline.quote: Two years later in 1861, Hiram Blood would purchase the dwelling just north of Stanton’s house and completely rebuild the structure so it could operate as a grocery store.

timeline.detail: Around the turn of the century Union Pacific Tea Shop sold imported teas here.
timeline.quote: At 23 Church Street Union Pacific Tea Shop offered teas from faraway places.

timeline.detail: A third story was added in 1906.
timeline.quote: Although the third story being added in 1906 and the 1920’s façade alterations hide all of the original details.

timeline.detail: White's Pure Milk took over from Union Pacific Tea in 1922.
timeline.quote: White’s Pure Milk took over Union Pacific Tea in 1922 and offered shoppers and array of dairy products.

timeline.detail: In 1926 the owners refaced the Italianate building in Art Deco style, adding stucco and a tile crest in the cornice.
timeline.quote: in 1926 when the owners of 23 Church Street renovated the façade of the old Italianate building to reflect the Art Deco style popular at the time.

timeline.detail: A 1952 McAllister photo shows renovations that remain today.
timeline.quote: Louis McAllister photograph taken in 1952 shows the renovations to 23 Church Street Those renovations remain today.

timeline.detail: Burlington Violin Co. occupied the building as of 2017.
timeline.quote: With the exceptions of Tina’s Home Design (19-21 Church) and Burlington Violin Co. (23 Church) the rest of the stores are large chains

photos.caption: Louis McAllister photograph taken in 1952 showing renovations to 23 Church Street
photos.credit: Louis L. McAllister Photographs, Box B18, Folder 27, Item 01

photos.caption: Then and now; possibly the oldest building on the block
photos.credit: Frank Wagner, University Landscape Change Program

timeline.what: New block with China Hall and shops
timeline.detail: A new building at what is now 19 Church held S.S. Brown's China Hall, G.L. Warner's grocery, Mrs. Brown's millinery and G.P. Wood's dry goods. The page dates it to the mid-19th century, and its Fig. 4 is an 1863 advertisement.
timeline.quote: the construction of a new building at what is now 19 Church Street truly exemplified Burlington in the mid-19th century. On one end was S.S. Brown’s “China Hall”

timeline.detail: Around the turn of the century Hope Outfitters sold clothing on credit, with Gauvin's photo studio upstairs.
timeline.quote: Hope Outfitters at 19-21 Church catered to both men and women, selling “made to wear” clothing

timeline.what: Cheerio Grill and The Hub Cigar Store
timeline.detail: The Cheerio Grill and The Hub Cigar Store arrived in the 1930s.
timeline.quote: The addition of the Cheerio Grill and The Hub Cigar Store in the 1930’s to 19-21

timeline.detail: A fire that started in The Hub Cigar Store grew to four alarms on April 9, 1945. Firefighters pulled the brick facade down with a winch.
timeline.quote: a small fire started in The Hub Cigar Store would grow to 4-alarm fire at 4 am on April 9th, 1945.

timeline.detail: A 1948 McAllister photo shows the lot still empty after the fire.
timeline.quote: 1948 Louis McAllister photograph looking south-west down Church St, showing the vacant lot at 19-21 Church left behind by the fire.

timeline.detail: Construction of the two-story concrete Irving Building began in 1953. The first tenant was Irving's clothing store.
timeline.quote: construction of a new building in 1953 would begin fill in the missing storefront left vacant almost a decade. The two-story Irving Building at 19-21 Church Street was constructed out of concrete with a flat roof.

timeline.detail: Tina's Home Design occupied the building as of 2017.
timeline.quote: With the exceptions of Tina’s Home Design (19-21 Church) and Burlington Violin Co. (23 Church) the rest of the stores are large chains

photos.credit: Oysters, Oysters. Burlington Free Press, 11/30/1863

photos.credit: 19-21 Church Street Fire, 4/9/1945, uvm.edu/landscape

photos.credit: Louis L. McAllister Photographs, Box A4, Folder 04, Item 2

timeline.what: Three-story brick block, Henry Greene furs
timeline.detail: In 1885 a three-story brick building replaced a two-story wooden one. Furrier Henry Greene was one of the first proprietors.
timeline.quote: In 1885 a three-story brick building replaced the two-story wooden structure at 11-17 Church Street One of the first proprietors was furrier Henry Greene.

timeline.detail: W.H. Zottman bought Greene's store at the start of the 20th century and ran a pharmacy at 17 Church for almost two decades.
timeline.quote: Zottman’s pharmacy would occupy 17 Church Street for almost two decades and was known for compounding prescriptions having the best soda fountain in the state.

timeline.detail: Preston's Jewelry arrived at 17 Church in 1917 and added a cantilevered sign.
timeline.quote: The arrival of Preston’s Jewelry store in 1917 to 17 Church Street would soon add the addition of a cantilevered sign over the street.

timeline.detail: Harry White opened a sporting goods shop at 11 Church in 1933 and added modern windows.
timeline.quote: Harry White, no relation to the milk proprietor, took over the space next Preston’s Jewelry and added new, modern, windows to the front of his new sporting goods shop in 1933.

timeline.detail: Federal Bake Shop came to 11 Church in 1943.
timeline.quote: Federal Bake Shop to 11 Church Street in 1943

timeline.detail: A 1963 winter fire destroyed the roof and top floor. The owner kept the ground floor and removed the top, leaving a four-bay, one-story building. Preston's reopened the next morning.
timeline.quote: The third fire to forever alter the architecture of the top block of Church Street would again happen in the middle of winter in 1963.

timeline.detail: Eddie Bauer added a concrete facade and parapet that remain as of 2017.
timeline.quote: the clothing chain Eddie Bauer adding a concrete façade and parapet to 11-17 Church that remain today.

photos.caption: Advertisement for Zottman's store, perfumes from around the globe
photos.credit: Zottman. Burlington Free Press, 12/20/1888

pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Top Block Project: Mid-Block East Side, by Danielle Allen, 2017

timeline.detail: An 1862 map shows a private office on the plot.
timeline.quote: An 1862 map indicates that the land once housed a private office.

timeline.detail: Before the current building, the plot held a small building housing George Perkins Marsh's personal library.
timeline.quote: Prior to construction, that same plot of land housed the personal library of local legend, George Perkins Marsh.

timeline.detail: The page says the 1869 Sanborn map shows 10 Church Street among the few buildings on this part of the block.
timeline.quote: the only buildings that occupied the eastern portion of the mid-block of Upper Church Street were 10 Church Street

timeline.what: Current building built for Hoyt E. Salls
timeline.detail: The current building was built in 1877 for Hoyt E. Salls.
timeline.quote: the current edifice at # 10 Church Street was built in 1877 for Mr. Hoyt E. Salls.

timeline.what: Millinery and arts and crafts store
timeline.detail: Through the turn of the 20th century it was retail space, including a millinery and an arts and crafts store.
timeline.quote: Through the turn of the twentieth century the building served as retail space and housed a variety of commercial enterprises including a millinery and an arts and crafts store.

timeline.what: Art Deco remodel, Abernethy's Men's Shop
timeline.detail: Frank D. Abernethy remodeled the facade in Art Deco style in 1936 and opened Abernethy's Men's Shop. It is one of few significant Art Deco buildings in Vermont.
timeline.quote: In 1936, the façade was remodeled to match the vision of the savvy businessman, Frank D. Abernethy, owner of Abernethy’s Department Store, next door.

timeline.what: E. B. Strong's Prime Steak House
timeline.detail: As of 2017 the storefront was E. B. Strong's Prime Steak House, open more than 30 years.
timeline.quote: Presently #10 Church Street’s storefront shop is currently home to E. B. Strong’s Prime Steak House Restaurant.

photos.caption: 10 Church Street
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, 2017

timeline.detail: The page says the building was built in 1872 as a six-bay Italianate structure.
timeline.quote: Built in 1872, the structure was formerly a delicate six-bay Italianate structure.

timeline.detail: The page also says construction began in 1873 when Joseph Chauvin bought the property. Chauvin lived upstairs and leased the ground floor.
timeline.quote: Construction on the site began in 1873, when the property was purchased by Joseph Chauvin.

timeline.detail: George W. Kelley ran a grocery here into the early 1900s.
timeline.quote: Through the following decades and into the early 1900s, George W. Kelley ran his grocery store from that address.

timeline.detail: By 1900 architect Louis Xavier Fremau added a single-bay building on the north side for his father's jewelry shop.
timeline.quote: By 1900, a single-bay building was added onto the north side of #14 Church Street by architect Louis Xavier Fremau.

timeline.detail: The southernmost shop housed the Casino Theater from 1912. A March 18, 1916 ad offered the theater for sale.
timeline.quote: From 1912, the southernmost shop in the block housed something rather remarkable, the new Casino Theater.

timeline.detail: A December 1983 fire heavily damaged the second and third floors. The current plain brick facade is from the rebuild.
timeline.quote: the original facade suffered damage in a fire in December of 1983. The second and third floors of the building were heavily damaged.

timeline.detail: Chris Sharp's bronze statue of Big Joe Burrell was unveiled in front of 16 Church on June 4, 2010.
timeline.quote: on June 4th, 2010, the opening night of Burlington’s 27th annual Discover Jazz Festival, Chris Sharp’s bronze sculpture of Big Joe Burrell was unveiled.

timeline.what: Crow Bookshop and Halverson's Upstreet Cafe
timeline.detail: As of 2017, Crow Bookshop was at 14 and Halverson's Upstreet Cafe at 16.
timeline.quote: Presently, the ground level of #14 Church Street boasts a lovely independent bookshop called Crow Bookshop and #16 Church Street is home to Halverson’s Upstreet Café.

photos.caption: Front elevation of 14-16 Church Street
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, September 2017

photos.caption: Big Joe Burrell statue

timeline.detail: The page says the 1869 Sanborn map shows a small market around 20 Church Street.
timeline.quote: a small market around 20 Church Street

timeline.detail: Bacon's Block at 22 Church was built in 1874 in high Italianate style, designed by E. C. Ryder for developer Nelson Bacon.
timeline.quote: Constructed in 1874, the edifice once known as “Bacon’s Block” at #22 Church Street is an attractive example of high style, Italianate architecture.

timeline.detail: First-floor tenants included M. V. B. Weeks, boots and shoes, a fancy goods store and a grocer, with apartments upstairs.
timeline.quote: Among the occupants on the first floor were Mr. M. V. B. Weeks, a dealer in boots and shoes, a fancy goods store, and a grocer.

timeline.detail: As of 2017 the block kept its historic facade and held shops including Little Citizen and Earthbound Trading Company, plus offices and apartments.
timeline.quote: continues to house an eclectic collection of novelty shops such as Little Citizen, Earthbound Trading Company, medical and commercial offices as well as apartments.

photos.caption: View looking east of #22 Church Street
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, September 2017

photos.caption: Louis McAllister photograph, December 3, 1936
photos.credit: Courtesy of UVM Special Collections

timeline.detail: The site began as a private residence and blacksmith shop in 1860. The page separately says the 1869 Sanborn map shows a paint shop near 28 Church.
timeline.quote: What began as a private residence and blacksmith shop in the 1860

timeline.detail: Through the 1860s the plot held a two-story market. The current building's foundation went in in 1875.
timeline.quote: Throughout the 1860s the plot housed a two-story market and in 1875 the foundation for the current building was erected.

timeline.detail: In 1889 the building was expanded with modern amenities and a third story.
timeline.quote: In 1889, the building was expanded through the addition of modern amenities and a third story.

timeline.detail: A 1955 remodel gave it the white enamel International style facade still present.
timeline.quote: the edifice went through one final remodel in 1955 that resulted in the sleek International style façade that is still present today.

timeline.what: Vermont Distillers and Vermont Flannel Company
timeline.detail: As of 2017 the ground floor was shared by Vermont Distillers and the Vermont Flannel Company.
timeline.quote: Today the ground floor store front is shared by two local businesses, Vermont Distillers and the Vermont Flannel Company.

photos.caption: #28 Church Street
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, September 2017

timeline.detail: The page says the 1869 Sanborn map shows a private residence near 30 Church Street.
timeline.quote: and a private residence near 30 Church Street.

timeline.detail: The 1900 Sanborn map shows a modest two-story structure.
timeline.quote: In 1900, a Sanborn Fire map shows a modest two-story structure at #30 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Jeremiah W. O'Sullivan commissioned the Classical Revival block in 1915, designed by Frank Lyman Austin.
timeline.quote: the contemporary building at #30 Church Street was built at the height of World War I, in 1915. The building was commissioned by the prominent businessman Jeremiah W. O’Sullivan and designed by architect Frank Lyman Austin.

timeline.detail: O'Sullivan's Pharmacy ran here from 1915 to 1922, later known as Liggett's Rexall Drugs.
timeline.quote: From 1915 to 1922, the building was the site of O’Sullivan’s Pharmacy. Later known as Liggett’s Rexall Drugs

timeline.detail: Various retailers used it from the 1940s through the 1990s. The ground floor facade was remodeled in the 1990s.
timeline.quote: It was during the 1990’s that the ground floor façade was remodeled, which accounts for the building’s current contemporary feel.

timeline.what: Statement's Hair Design and David's Tea
timeline.detail: As of 2017 it held Statement's Hair Design and David's Tea behind a teal storefront.
timeline.quote: Today the building is recognized for its colorful teal storefront and is the location of Statement’s Hair Design and David’s Tea.

photos.caption: #30 Church Street
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, September 2017

timeline.detail: A plaque dates 32 Church to 1854, making it one of the oldest original buildings on the street.
timeline.quote: A small plaque on the front elevation displays the building’s vintage, built in 1854.

timeline.detail: It was named Warner House for Charles Warner, who bought it in 1862.
timeline.quote: It was historically given the name Warner House, in honor of Charles Warner, who purchased the property in 1862.

timeline.what: Bakery, then Thomas and Company Clothing
timeline.detail: In the early 20th century it held a bakery and later Thomas and Company Clothing, which with Sheppard and Hammel lasted into the 1980s.
timeline.quote: During in the early twentieth century records show that the site housed a bakery, and later the Thomas and Company Clothing Shop.

timeline.detail: Clothing retail continued until fall 2017, when Bertha Church's Intimate Apparel moved elsewhere on Church Street.
timeline.quote: The site continued to honor its long tradition of retail clothing sales until the fall of 2017, when Bertha Church’s Intimate Apparel moved to another location further down Church Street.

timeline.detail: As of 2017 the upper floor, 34 Church, held Silver Threads Tailoring.
timeline.quote: The building’s upper floor, #34 Church Street, still houses Silver Threads Tailoring.

photos.caption: 2, 34, and 32 1/2 Church Street (caption as given)
photos.credit: Danielle Allen, September 2017

pages.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018

timeline.detail: The Concert Hall Building stood on the southeast corner of Church and Cherry at least as early as 1830, based on the 1830 and 1853 maps.
timeline.quote: it was standing as least as early as 1830, based on comparisons of the 1830 Ammi B. Young map and the 1853 Presdee & Edwards map.

timeline.detail: An 1860 ad placed the Burlington Sentinel office on Concert Hall's ground floor, between two stores.
timeline.quote: an 1860 ad for the Burlington Sentinel describes their office as “on the ground floor of Concert Hall, between the stores of C.F. Staniford and C.W. Wingate.”

timeline.detail: A February 1863 ad placed H.M. Phelps' marble works in the Concert Hall building under the Times office. The 1862 Wainwright map also shows the marble works here.
timeline.quote: a February 1863 ad for H.M. Phelps’ marble works, which listed his business as “in Concert Hall building under the Times Office.”

timeline.detail: Soon after, Concert Hall burned or was demolished. Gunsmith Edward H. Payn built a three-story Italianate block. Masonry was nearly done by December 1863 and the interior near finished in April 1864.
timeline.quote: By December of the same year, the masonry work was nearly finished, and workers had begun removing the scaffolding.

timeline.detail: An April 1864 notice said the interior would soon be finished.
timeline.quote: Four months later, in April of 1864, another notice announced that the interior would soon be finished.

timeline.detail: The Free Press reported on August 19, 1864 that local Democrats rented a room in Payn's Block for weekly meetings.
timeline.quote: On August 19th, 1864, the Press noted that “the local Democrats have organized recently, whether as “Knights of the Golden Circle,” “American Knights,” or under some other title, we are not informed. They have rented a room in Payn’s Block

timeline.what: E.H. Payn's gun and engraving shop
timeline.detail: Payn expanded his business, adding engraving, locksmithing and stenciling in 1867, three employees by 1869, and two branch locations in 1879.
timeline.quote: In 1867, he changed his title from that of simply gunsmith to include engraving, locksmithing, and stenciling.

timeline.detail: An independent commercial college, founded in 1878, occupied the building until 1887.
timeline.quote: the Commercial College, which was founded in 1878 and left the building the same year as Payn.

timeline.detail: Payn sold his space at 38 Church in 1887 to the American Clothing Company's Red 46 Department Store, which grew to own all of Payn's Block and half of Nelson's Block. It closed in the late 1920s.
timeline.quote: In 1887, Payn consolidated his various offices and sold his space at 38 Church Street to the American Clothing Company’s Red 46 Department Store, managed by Robert and Mrs. F. Levin.

timeline.detail: Red 46 built a rear addition in 1910 that nearly doubled the first floor's length.
timeline.quote: The first was in 1910, when they built a major rear addition that nearly doubled the length of the first floor.

timeline.detail: In 1917 the upper floors were gutted and rearranged into show rooms.
timeline.quote: The second came in 1917, when the upper floors were gutted and rearranged to create better show rooms.

timeline.detail: The pressed metal facade uniting Payn's and Nelson's Blocks was added c. 1925.
timeline.quote: the current pressed metal facade was added to both Payn’s and Nelson’s Blocks circa 1925 to unite the two buildings.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 Payn's Block housed Dear Lucy, Pokiworks and Uncommon Grounds.
timeline.quote: Today, Payn’s Block houses Dear Lucy, Pokiworks, and Uncommon Grounds.

photos.caption: Stereoview of Payn's Block between 1878 and 1887, from Cherry and Church
photos.credit: Courtesy of Special Collections, University of Vermont

photos.caption: Payn's Block today, viewed from the southwest
photos.credit: Photo taken by Chris Rizer, 2018

timeline.detail: In 1862 furniture maker Henry J. Nelson and grocer Augustus Barrows owned neighboring buildings on the lot, each under a decade old.
timeline.quote: they owned neighboring buildings on the lot in 1862, which themselves were less than a decade old

timeline.detail: The three-story Italianate block was likely built in 1866, as it first appears in the 1867 directory.
timeline.quote: was likely built in 1866. There are few details concerning its construction, but as it is first mentioned in the 1867 city directory, it was likely finished soon before.

timeline.detail: Barrows was among the first businesses in 1867 and left by 1885, replaced by a dry goods store and others.
timeline.quote: Barrows’ business left the building by 1885 and was replaced by a dry goods store and others

timeline.detail: Nelson's business stayed until his death in April 1910. The building was then sold to the American Clothing Company.
timeline.quote: Nelson’s business, on the other hand, remained in the building up until his death in April of 1910, after which it was also sold to the American Clothing Company

timeline.detail: Red 46 Department Store expanded into the building in 1906.
timeline.quote: eventually leading to the Red 46 Department Store’s expansion into the space in 1906.

timeline.detail: The pressed metal facade shared with Payn's Block was added c. 1925.
timeline.quote: the current pressed metal facade was added to both Payn’s and Nelson’s Blocks circa 1925 to unite the two buildings.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the block held the Catamount Store and Fjallraven Burlington.
timeline.quote: Today, Nelson’s Block is home to the Catamount Store and Fjällräven Burlington.

photos.caption: Nelson's Block today, viewed from the southwest
photos.credit: Photo taken by Chris Rizer, 2018

timeline.detail: The 1830 Ammi B. Young map shows the Chittenden County House, the County Jail and a barn on this lot.
timeline.quote: The first known buildings on this lot, as early as the 1830 Ammi B. Young map, were the Chittenden County House, where the county sheriff/jailor lived, County Jail, and an associated barn.

timeline.detail: The frame buildings were all destroyed by fire on January 29, 1851.
timeline.quote: they were all destroyed by fire on January 29th, 1851.

timeline.detail: A new brick County House and Jail and a new barn were completed by 1853. Between 1862 and 1869 the jail was remodeled and almost doubled.
timeline.quote: a new brick County House and Jail and replacement of the barn, both of which were completed by 1853.

timeline.detail: Poorly maintained, the jail stood until 1887, when the lot was sold for $12,000 to a company owned by Augustus Barrows, Lewis M. Barrows and H.L. Bundy.
timeline.quote: That buyer, at a price of $12,000, was a real estate corporation owned by Augustus Barrows, Lewis M. Barrows, and H.L. Bundy.

timeline.detail: Barrows and Bundy finished a four-story commercial block in April 1888 for about $30,000, with stores, tenements and a fourth-floor ballroom.
timeline.quote: Barrows and Bundy then put up a four-story commercial block at a cost of approximately $30,000, which was finished in April of 1888.

timeline.detail: The largest tenants were Miles and McMahon's Boots and Shoes and the Boston Store, filling most of the first two floors.
timeline.quote: Of the commercial interests in the building, by far the two largest were Miles and McMahon’s Boots & Shoes and the Boston Store, owned by M.J. Leo and P.F. McLaren.

timeline.detail: After Augustus Barrows died in 1897, the J.W. McAuslan Company bought the Boston Store and the building.
timeline.quote: until 1897, at which point Augustus Barrows died and the J.W. McAuslan Company bought the Boston Store and the rest of the building.

timeline.what: Fisher Bros, then Rutland Combination Cash Store
timeline.detail: The Boston Store was sold in 1908 to the Fisher Bros, who sold it to the Rutland Combination Cash Store. A tenement fire during their ownership was quickly put out.
timeline.quote: They continued operating the Boston Store until 1908, when it was sold to the Fisher Bros, who then sold it to the Rutland Combination Cash Store.

timeline.what: Green Brothers' Store, destroyed by fire
timeline.detail: The Green Brothers' Store ran the building until a 1929 fire destroyed it.
timeline.quote: The building was then sold to the Green Brothers’ Store, who operated it until a fire destroyed the building in 1929.

photos.caption: Circa 1890 view of Church Street showing the Barrows Block soon after its 1888 construction

timeline.detail: After the 1929 fire Montgomery Ward bought half the lot and built a two-story store to a standard company design, opening December 28. It closed in 1961.
timeline.quote: the 1929 Montgomery Ward Building (#52-54) and a modern commercial building (#56-58).

timeline.detail: Since the 1961 closure the building has hosted a number of businesses.
timeline.quote: Since the department store’s closure in 1961, it has hosted a number of businesses.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 it housed Designer's Circle and Homeport.
timeline.quote: Today, it is home to Designer’s Circle and Homeport.

photos.caption: The Montgomery Ward Building, viewed from the southwest
photos.credit: Photo taken by Chris Rizer in 2018

timeline.detail: The 1974 fire that destroyed Stetson's Row also destroyed the southern half of the old jail and Barrows Block lot.
timeline.quote: This is the southern half of the Jail and Barrows Block Lot, which was destroyed along with Stetson's Row in the 1974 fire.

timeline.detail: A concrete block building with brick veneer was built in 1976. It housed Banana Republic as of 2018.
timeline.quote: The first, built in 1976, filled the other half of the Barrows lot as was previously mentioned, and currently houses Banana Republic.

photos.caption: #56 Church Street, viewed from the west
photos.credit: Photo taken by Chris Rizer, 2018

timeline.detail: In 1830 this was the most developed part of the block, with three brick buildings. A fourth store was added before 1851.
timeline.quote: In 1830, this was the most developed section of the block, known as Stetson’s Row or Stetson’s Block and home to three brick buildings.

timeline.detail: The January 1851 fire that destroyed the County Jail began in a cellar at the south end near Bank Street and destroyed the row. Twelve families lost their homes.
timeline.quote: A fourth store was added between then and 1851, but it was for naught, as the same fire that destroyed the County Jail destroyed Stetson’s Row as well.

timeline.detail: By 1869 the row was rebuilt and expanded as three frame buildings with six businesses.
timeline.quote: Yet, by 1869, the entire row had been rebuilt and expanded in the fashionable Italianate style. That year, the Row consisted of three frame buildings that housed six businesses.

timeline.what: W.W. Wood's Boots and Shoes and neighbors
timeline.detail: Tenants from 60 Church southward were W.W. Wood's Boots and Shoes, C. Storrs and Son's Market, David Valpee's shoemaking, a milliner, Henry A. Mooney's Boots and Shoes, and Moody Haskell's shop and home.
timeline.quote: Beginning at 60 Church Street and working south, they were W.W. Wood’s Boots & Shoes, C. Storrs and Son’s Market, David Valpee’s shoemaking, a milliner, Henry A. Mooney’s Boots & Shoes, and Moody Haskell’s shop and home.

timeline.detail: By 1889 W.W. Wood had rebuilt his store in brick with a third story, and the four southern businesses had been joined into one mass.
timeline.quote: Twenty years later, in 1889, expansion was still ongoing on Stetson’s Row. W.W. Wood had rebuilt his store in brick and added a third story.

timeline.detail: Mary Currier's Ladies Clothing Store at 66 Church was rebuilt in brick. Otherwise little changed until 1974.
timeline.quote: the rebuilding of Mary Currier’s Ladies Clothing Store at 66 Church Street in brick

timeline.detail: A 1974 fire destroyed all of Stetson's Row, roughly the same area as in 1851.
timeline.quote: That year, disaster struck yet again, and a fire destroyed essentially the same area that it had in 1851.

timeline.detail: A small two-story shopping center with four or so businesses was built in 1976.
timeline.quote: The other, built in the same year, is a small two-story shopping center that houses four or so businesses.
